subject: Throughput surface modeling for Luma Health - Dedicated sizing request
messages:
From: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@lumahealth.com>
To: Priya Natarajan <priya@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>
Cc: Sarah Ng <sarah.ng@lumahealth.com>
Date: Fri, 4 Sep 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Luma - workload profile & ask for Dedicated throughput mapping

Hi Priya / Ben —

Thanks again for the demo last week. Procurement looped me in to get concrete numbers so we can size a Reserved Dedicated slab for our pilot. Attached is a simple token profile from our staging traffic (luma_token_profile.csv) — a few important points to highlight:

- Model family: MPT/LLM-2-ish (we'll call it a 13B-ish autoregressive workload for now)
- Typical prompt + completion: ~350 tokens median, 1,100 tokens high tail (rare)
- Expected peak QPS (external): ~120 concurrent requests during day spike windows (12:00–14:00 PT)
- Latency target: p95 <= 600 ms for user-facing flows; background batch can be looser
- Multi-tenant routes: about 60% of traffic needs dedicated isolation, 40% can accept regional fallback

Can you produce a lightweight throughput -> GPU mapping (tokens/sec estimates per GPU for the model variant) and a short headroom recommendation for the initial commit? We need:

1) Tokens/sec per GPU baseline (assume 350-token avg) and p95 latency fit for the 600 ms SLO
2) Recommended commit slab (GPU count + cushion %) for the pilot to cover daytime spikes and 2-week load growth
3) Burst/fallback playbook: what happens if Dedicated capacity saturates?

We're aiming to get procurement numbers this cycle — any quick table is helpful.

Appended to this thread: our procurement contact (procurement@lumahealth.com).

Thanks,
Tom

Tom Reynolds
Head of Integrations — Luma Health

From: Priya Natarajan <priya@redwood.ai>
To: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@lumahealth.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 4 Sep 2026 12:37:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Luma - workload profile & ask for Dedicated throughput mapping

Tom —

Appreciate the token profile — good detail. Attaching a quick SLO fit matrix (slo_fit_matrix_v1.xlsx) and a short note below with our initial surface-level estimates. This is intended to be a conservative starting point before we model queueing and batching in more detail.

High-level assumptions used (explicit so procurement has context):
- Model: 13B autoregressive variant (FP16 equivalent path)
- Avg tokens per request used for math: 350 tokens
- Measurement: tokens/sec budget for p95 ~ 600 ms target (includes network + service overhead)
- Continuous batching efficiency: 1.15x baseline (can increase for very bursty workloads)

Initial estimates (ballpark for sizing):
- Single A100-style GPU (dedicated inference profile) sustained tokens/sec: ~2200 tok/s at target p95 (350-token median)
- Effective user-facing requests/sec per GPU (350 tokens/request): ~6.3 req/s (2200 / 350)
- Peak window demand (120 concurrent reqs): assuming average 6s server-side processing per req without batching — this maps to ~20 req/s system-wide; but with concurrency and variable in-flight requests we size for token throughput rather than per-request concurrency.

Recommended commit slab for pilot (three options):
- Conservative (low risk): 12 GPUs (covers peak + 40% headroom) — rationale: 12 GPUs * 2200 tok/s = 26,400 tok/s -> ~75 req/s equivalent; accommodates growth and quantization risks
- Balanced (cost-aware): 9 GPUs (covers peak + 20% headroom)
- Aggressive (cost-minimal): 7 GPUs (tight, rely on fallback for 10–20% of bursts)

Burst/fallback playbook (short):
- 1) Autoscale to regional extra capacity (if allowed in contract) — compatible model variants used to keep latency under control
- 2) Route non-critical traffic to shared-hosted tier (40% of traffic acceptable)
- 3) Apply short-duration request throttling / token caps for extremely long completions

Open questions for you that will change the numbers:
- Can you confirm worst-case average token length during peak (350 is median; p90/p95 higher?)
- Do you accept a small fraction of requests routed to hosted fallback during spikes?

If helpful, we can run a short throughput simulation with your exact token distribution and return a more formal "throughput surface" matrix (tokens/sec vs % tail latency vs GPU count). Would you like to schedule 30 minutes next week?

Thanks — I'll loop in Ethan (plat-ops) to sanity-check the GPU sku mapping once you confirm.

Best,
Priya
Director, Sales Engineering — Redwood Inference

From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Luma - workload profile & ask for Dedicated throughput mapping

Tom / Priya — quick follow-up with a slightly more operational view and a conservative GPU mapping so Procurement has a clear ask.

Notes and quick math (conservative knobs):
- Practical sustained tokens/sec per A100 equiv (conservative accounting for p95, KV cache misses, tail completion cost): 1,850 tok/s
- Effective req/s per GPU (350 tokens avg): ~5.3 req/s
- Continuous batching multiplier: we usually see 1.1–1.3x in production; use 1.2x for optimistic planning, 1.1x for procurement budgets

Suggested Dedicated slab for initial 12-week pilot:
- Nominal: 10 GPUs (covers expected peak + ~30% cushion)
- If procurement insists on round numbers or higher cushion: 12 GPUs (recommended for low-friction ops)

Rationale / bullet tradeoffs:
- 10 GPUs * 1,850 tok/s = 18,500 tok/s -> with 1.2x batching this is ~22,200 tok/s effective
- That gives ~63 req/s equivalent at 350 tok/request, which covers a daytime peak of 120 concurrent requests if client-side concurrency averages around 1.8–2.0 active requests per user (many customers use client-side batching).
- Quantized 8-bit runtime profile could raise tok/s per GPU by ~25% but we keep that as a post-onboard optimization

Procurement language suggestions: include a short burst SLA (30s allowance) and an agreed fallback to hosted pool if Dedicated saturates beyond N minutes. That avoids interruption while we spin up reserve capacity.

Happy to spin a short sheet that shows GPU count vs tokens/sec vs cost/month — Priya, if you want, I can draft that and share by EOD Tuesday.

—Ben
Senior Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference
